note: CETP inhibition to raise HDL-C in high-cardiovascular-risk hyperlipidaemia: the cholesterol-fed rabbit predicted less atherosclerosis, patients got none (torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, evacetrapib) or a modest benefit attributed to LDL lowering (anacetrapib), plus torcetrapib's unforeseen off-target aldosterone/blood-pressure toxicity; obicetrapib's outcome trial had not published as of Nov 2026.
label: Hyperlipidemia (CETP)

engagement.note: JTT-705 (dalcetrapib) raised HDL-C and lowered non-HDL-C in cholesterol-fed rabbits: first in-vivo small-molecule CETP inhibitor.
engagement.quote: Here we describe CETP inhibitors that form a disulphide bond with CETP, and present one such inhibitor (JTT-705) that increases HDL cholesterol, decreases non-HDL cholesterol and inhibits the progression of atherosclerosis in rabbits.

engagement.note: JTT-705 900 mg cut CETP activity 37% and raised HDL-C 34% in 198 mildly hyperlipidaemic volunteers, as the rabbit predicted.
engagement.quote: We show that the use of the CETP inhibitor JTT-705 in humans is an effective means to raise HDL cholesterol levels with minor gastrointestinal side effects (P=0.06).
engagement.reason: HDL rose in humans as in rabbits
engagement.judgement: The abstract itself puts rabbit and human side by side ('In earlier studies, JTT-705 ... was shown to increase plasma HDL cholesterol and to inhibit the progression of atherosclerosis in cholesterol-fed rabbits. This study describes the first results ... in humans'), so comparison_stated=true. Abstract-level only (Circulation full text refused the fetch); the rabbit percentage could not be verified, so magnitude is direction_only. Subjects were healthy volunteers with mild hyperlipidaemia, not patients. Pre-registry era: no NCT record.

dose.note: Rabbits were dosed to deep CETP inhibition (torcetrapib 70-80%, 2007); no published comparison of that exposure target with patient exposure was found.
dose.quote: Here we describe CETP inhibitors that form a disulphide bond with CETP, and present one such inhibitor (JTT-705) that increases HDL cholesterol, decreases non-HDL cholesterol and inhibits the progression of atherosclerosis in rabbits.
dose.judgement: Model numbers from Morehouse 2007 (https://doi.org/10.1194/jlr.M600332-JLR200, abstract): torcetrapib inhibited rabbit CETP activity 70-80% and raised HDL-C >=3-fold (207 vs 57 mg/dL), giving 60% less aortic atherosclerosis. Patient doses were set on human HDL response, not on the rabbit's inhibition level: dalcetrapib 900 mg gave 37% CETP inhibition (de Grooth 2002) and the 600 mg outcome dose raised HDL-C 31-40% (dal-OUTCOMES); torcetrapib 60 mg raised HDL-C ~61% (ILLUSTRATE). Nobody published a rabbit-vs-patient exposure/occupancy comparison that I could find, so untested; the common claim that dalcetrapib was under-dosed relative to the rabbit is not sourced here.

efficacy.note: JTT-705 inhibited aortic atherosclerosis in cholesterol-fed rabbits, the experiment that justified HDL-raising by CETP inhibition.
efficacy.quote: Here we describe CETP inhibitors that form a disulphide bond with CETP, and present one such inhibitor (JTT-705) that increases HDL cholesterol, decreases non-HDL cholesterol and inhibits the progression of atherosclerosis in rabbits.

efficacy.note: Torcetrapib raised HDL-C 61% but did not slow coronary atheroma (ILLUSTRATE); ILLUMINATE then showed more deaths and events.
efficacy.quote: It was also associated with an increase in blood pressure, and there was no significant decrease in the progression of coronary atherosclerosis.
efficacy.judgement: Rabbit (Morehouse 2007, torcetrapib itself: aortic atherosclerosis 60% lower at >=3x HDL-C) vs patients (ILLUSTRATE IVUS: percent atheroma volume +0.12% vs +0.19%, P=0.72, at +61% HDL-C) - a null, so off_by_>5x and the source calls it 'lack of efficacy'. The NEJM abstract does not itself name the rabbit, so comparison_stated=false; the primary source that states the comparison in print is Forrest 2008 (https://doi.org/10.1038/bjp.2008.229, read in full): 'preclinical studies with CETP inhibitors demonstrated beneficial antiatherosclerotic effects in animal models' followed by ILLUMINATE's 'unexpected increase in cardiovascular events and death'. Same-year confirmations: RADIANCE 1 cIMT null (Kastelein 2007, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa071359) and ILLUMINATE (Barter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0706628; events HR 1.25, death HR 1.58; NCT00134264, no registry results). Later, status unchanged: dal-OUTCOMES 2012 tested the exact molecule from the 2000 rabbit experiment (dalcetrapib, HR 1.04, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1206797; NCT00658515 results posted 2020-01-03); ACCELERATE 2017 evacetrapib HR 1.01 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1609581; NCT01687998 results 2018-05-16); REVEAL 2017 anacetrapib RR 0.91 with the effect attributed to non-HDL lowering (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1706444; NCT01252953 results 2018-05-04). Contra overrides. Human genetics pointed the other way before the rabbit was built on: CETP-deficiency carriers had MORE CHD (Zhong 1996, https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI118751), but the class relied on the rabbit, so the rabbit is the best model here. ILLUSTRATE itself: NCT00134173, no registry results posted.

safety.note: The rabbit (and the 2007 torcetrapib rabbit study) measured lipids and lesions only; no blood-pressure or adrenal end-point was reported.
safety.quote: Here we describe CETP inhibitors that form a disulphide bond with CETP, and present one such inhibitor (JTT-705) that increases HDL cholesterol, decreases non-HDL cholesterol and inhibits the progression of atherosclerosis in rabbits.

safety.note: Torcetrapib raised systolic BP 5.4 mmHg and aldosterone and increased deaths (HR 1.58); the preclinical models had flagged nothing.
safety.quote: Although there was evidence of an off-target effect of torcetrapib, we cannot rule out adverse effects related to CETP inhibition.
safety.judgement: The model's silence did not hold: no CETP-inhibitor preclinical paper reported blood pressure or aldosterone before patients showed SBP +5.4 mmHg, lower potassium, higher sodium/bicarbonate/aldosterone and death HR 1.58 (ILLUMINATE abstract; NEJM paywalled, NCT00134264 has no posted results). The NEJM abstract does not compare with a model, so comparison_stated=false. The primary source that states the comparison and finds the off-target mechanism is Forrest 2008 (https://doi.org/10.1038/bjp.2008.229, open access, read in full): torcetrapib acutely raised blood pressure in CETP-null and CETP-transgenic mice, rats, dogs and rhesus monkeys and released aldosterone from rat adrenocortical cells, while anacetrapib did neither at equal exposure - 'The blood pressure response to torcetrapib is independent of inhibition of CETP.' So the signal was detectable in ordinary species once anyone looked; the class's efficacy models never looked. Forrest 2008 also predicted anacetrapib would be clean, and REVEAL 2017 found no excess death - a later matched prediction, but contra overrides.
